strengths: The paper makes a meaningful and well-motivated extension of the soft-label Bayes error estimation framework of Ishida et al. (2023): the fine-grained bias analysis (Theorem 1) genuinely improves the prior bound by removing the unnatural dependence on n and revealing a separation-adaptive decay rate (mixture of 1/m and 1/sqrt(m)), which is validated empirically with clear log-log slope analysis in Section B.3.

The second contribution — Bayes error estimation from corrupted soft labels — is a new and practically relevant problem setting (labeling distribution shift, human/LLM annotator subjectivity), and the observation that calibration guarantees alone are insufficient (Example 2) is an instructive negative result.

The consistency result via isotonic calibration (Theorem 2) is technically solid. The proof apparatus (sharp oracle inequality for binary isotonic regression under misspecification, Proposition 2; metric entropy bound, Theorem 4) is carefully developed and the theoretical requirement (only the ordering of soft labels is preserved) is a genuine relaxation of the clean-label assumption.
The instance-free nature of the method is practically valuable (privacy-constrained settings, high-dimensional data), and the paper clearly articulates this advantage.

Experiments cover synthetic data with controlled corruption and two real-world soft-labeled datasets (CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H), comparing multiple calibration baselines (isotonic, histogram binning with several bin counts, beta calibration), with bootstrap confidence intervals and code availability.
The paper is honest about limitations (e.g., unverifiable monotone corruption assumption, unaddressed violation of f' >= c, difficulty of validating estimates without ground truth).
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental over Ishida et al. (2023): both contributions refine or extend a single prior work rather than opening a substantially new direction, which limits the potential impact.

The key theoretical assumption for the corrupted-label setting — that corrupted soft labels are a deterministic monotone transformation of the clean ones (η̃ = f(η)) — is strong and fundamentally unverifiable in practice. The real-world experiments (CIFAR-10H treated as 'corrupted') do not and cannot check whether this ordering assumption holds, so the practical applicability of the guarantee is uncertain.

The worst-case rate of the proposed estimator (n^{-1/3}) is slow, constants in the bounds are unspecified or unknown, and there is no analysis of what happens when the monotonicity assumption is violated (the authors explicitly state they have 'not yet reached a theoretical understanding'), leaving a significant theoretical gap.

Evaluation is narrow: binary classification only, one 2D synthetic distribution for the main experiments, and indirect validation on real data (comparing estimates against a ViT/ResNet test error, which itself is only a loose reference point). No comparison against alternative correction strategies beyond calibration methods, and no experiment demonstrating the computable bias bound (Corollary 2) on real data.

The observation that perfect calibration is insufficient (Example 2) is fairly obvious given the known gap between calibration and full probabilistic accuracy, and the superiority of isotonic over beta calibration, while empirically interesting, is only conjecturally explained.

Real-world experiments cannot access 'clean' soft labels (acknowledged), so the accuracy of the proposed estimator on the most practically relevant scenarios remains unverified; the paper's headline claim of 'practical estimation' is therefore supported somewhat indirectly.

strengths: The paper is technically sound: the proofs (bias bounds via sharpened Jensen inequalities, high-probability risk bounds for binary isotonic regression) are careful and appear correct.
The observation that calibration guarantees alone are insufficient (Example 2) is a clean and instructive result, and the choice of isotonic calibration is well-motivated by the theory.

Theorem 1 provides a genuinely tighter bias bound than Ishida et al. (2023), removing the unnatural dependence on n and characterizing an adaptive mixture of 1/m and 1/sqrt(m) decay rates, which is validated by numerical experiments.
Writing is clear and well-organized, with detailed proofs in the appendix and code made available.
The practical motivation (instance-free estimation, privacy constraints, label distribution shift in CIFAR-10H, LLM annotators) is real and relevant.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and incremental: the paper is essentially a follow-up to Ishida et al. (2023). Theorem 1 follows fairly directly from known Jensen-gap (Gao et al., 2019) and Lipschitz/Hoeffding arguments, and the isotonic regression machinery is adapted from standard results (Zhang 2002, Bellec 2018, Yang & Barber 2019); Proposition 2 is a modest technical extension of these to the binary case.

The central assumption of Theorem 2 — that corrupted soft labels are deterministic monotone transforms of the clean ones (correct ordering preserved) — is strong and, crucially, unverifiable in the very real-world scenarios the paper motivates (LLM annotators, subjective human confidence, labeling shift). When the ordering assumption fails, no guarantee survives, which substantially limits practical significance.
Theorem 3 additionally requires f' >= c > 0, which is again restrictive; the paper admits there is no theory for violations and relies only on empirical observations in Section D.2.

The consistency rate n^{-1/3} is slow, so the guarantee is of limited practical value for realistic sample sizes; no finite-sample practical uncertainty quantification is derived for the proposed estimator.

The evaluation is narrow: only binary classification, two real-world datasets, and comparison baselines limited to alternative calibrators. There is no comparison against instance-based Bayes error estimators, and the real-data experiments lack ground truth — validation against a classifier's test error is only an upper-bound sanity check, so the paper cannot actually demonstrate accuracy of its estimates on real data (acknowledged by the authors but still a significant limitation).
The method requires both corrupted soft labels and a hard label per instance for calibration, doubling annotation cost in practice; this cost trade-off is not discussed.
The empirical conclusions (e.g., hist-25 failure on Fashion-MNIST, beta calibration underperformance) are anecdotal and not connected back to theory, leaving the practical guidance weak.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored question: estimating the Bayes error when only corrupted (rather than clean) soft labels are available, extending the line of work by Ishida et al. (2023) in a meaningful direction.

The theoretical contribution on the bias of the hard-label-based estimator (Theorem 1) is clean and genuinely improves the prior bound: it removes the dependence on n, shows the estimator's upper bias is zero (one-sided), and reveals an adaptive decay rate that mixes O(1/m) and O(1/sqrt(m)) depending on class separation. The computable bound in Corollary 2 (200x tighter on binarized CIFAR-10) is a nice practical payoff.

The observation that calibration is necessary but not sufficient (Example 2: a perfectly calibrated constant predictor gives a badly biased Bayes error estimate) is an insightful and well-motivated point that elevates the paper beyond a simple plug-in proposal.

The main theoretical result (Theorem 2) providing a consistent estimator under only an ordering assumption (monotone corruption) is elegant; the derivation via a new risk bound for binary isotonic regression under model misspecification (Proposition 2, with metric-entropy and localized-width arguments) is technically solid and of independent interest.

The theory is validated empirically: the numerical experiments in B.3 confirm the predicted bias decay rates (slopes close to -1 and -0.5 in the appropriate regimes), and the main experiments (Fig. 4) on synthetic data, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-10H, and Fashion-MNIST support the practical viability of isotonic calibration, including the interesting negative result about well-specified beta calibration.

The instance-free property is well-motivated for privacy-sensitive applications, and the empirical finding that uncalibrated corrupted labels severely overestimate the Bayes error (Fig. 1) is a compelling motivating example.
The paper is generally well-written and clearly organized; proofs appear complete and the appendices are thorough.
weaknesses: The assumption underlying the main guarantee (Theorem 2: noiseless monotone corruption; Theorem 3: monotone corruption with f' >= c) is strong, and the paper admits there is no theoretical understanding of the behavior when it is violated - only empirical evidence (Section D.2). Since real corruption mechanisms (LLM annotator bias, subjective human confidence) may not preserve ordering, the practical applicability of the guarantee is limited.

Evaluation against ground truth on real-world datasets is fundamentally weak: the estimated Bayes error is compared only to a ViT/ResNet test error, which is merely an upper bound on the Bayes error. The authors acknowledge this, but it means the real-data experiments provide weak evidence that the estimates are accurate (they could, e.g., be underestimates that happen to fall below the classifier's test error).

The scope is confined to binary classification, while the motivating datasets are multiclass and were binarized by ad hoc class grouping; the multiclass extension (relevant given Jeong et al., 2023) is left as future work.

No comparison with alternative Bayes error estimation baselines (e.g., divergence-based methods of Berisha et al. 2014, Noshad et al. 2019, or normalizing-flow-based estimation of Theisen et al. 2021) in the experiments; comparisons are limited to variants of the soft-label estimator itself.

The method requires hard labels y_i drawn from the true posterior for each instance to perform calibration, which is an additional data requirement that partially undercuts the advantage over simply averaging m hard labels as in the prior work; a head-to-head cost analysis (labels needed per accuracy gain) is absent.

The contribution is an incremental extension of a single prior paper (Ishida et al., 2023); the individual technical ingredients (sharpened Jensen gap bounds, isotonic regression risk analysis) are mostly assembled from known tools, which limits novelty.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('CURRUPTED' in a section title, 'expeirments', 'indentify', 'resouces'), and the constant C in Theorem 2 is unspecified, making the bound hard to use for practical interval construction without further work.

strengths: The paper makes two solid and well-motivated theoretical contributions: (i) a sharp, distribution-adaptive bias bound for the hard-label-based Bayes error estimator (Theorem 1) that removes the unnatural dependence on n and reveals an instance-level decomposition between O(1/m) and O(1/sqrt(m)) decay rates, with a computable corollary (Corollary 2) that is shown to be over 200x tighter than the prior bound in a realistic setting; (ii) a novel and practically important problem formulation of Bayes error estimation from corrupted soft labels, with a consistency guarantee (Theorem 2) under the weak assumption that corruption is order-preserving.

The observation that 'calibration alone is not enough' (Example 2) is a crisp, insightful negative result that clarifies why isotonic regression specifically works, and the extension to noisy corruption (Theorem 3) connecting hard-label averaging to bounded-variance noise is natural and useful.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive: synthetic data with controllable corruption, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST/Fashion-MNIST-H, ChaosNLI, a new ICLR peer-review dataset, validation of the bias-decay theory in Appendix B.3, ablations on order-breakage severity via Kendall tau, and the use of the FeeBee framework to compare calibration algorithms on real data where ground truth is unavailable.

The instance-free property is practically valuable (privacy-sensitive scenarios, high-dimensional data), and the paper is honest about its limitations (e.g., Theorem 3's flat-derivative assumption, inability to run the 'clean' setup on real data).
Reproducibility is well addressed: full proofs in appendices, exact library versions, hardware details, code availability, and an LLM-usage disclosure.
weaknesses: The contribution is an incremental extension of a single prior work (Ishida et al., 2023). Theorem 1 builds directly on known Jensen-gap bounds (Gao et al., 2019) plus the concavity of phi_Err; the technical machinery is standard and the conceptual novelty is moderate, limited to binary classification.

The guarantees for corrupted soft labels rely on assumptions whose practical applicability is debatable: Theorem 2 requires exactly order-preserving corruption, and Theorem 3 requires f' >= c, which is hard to verify in practice (e.g., for LLM-generated confidences). The n^{-1/3} rate is also slow in absolute terms. The behavior when these assumptions are violated is studied only empirically, with no theoretical characterization.

The new ICLR peer-review dataset introduces methodological concerns: using the overall acceptance rate as the Bayes error upper bound E is crude, the assumption that normalized review scores form a corrupted (monotone) version of true posteriors is untestable, and mixing conferences from 2017-2025 raises distribution-shift issues that the paper does not analyze.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the statement that isotonic calibration 'performed the best across all datasets' is based on FeeBee scores whose sensitivity to the choice of E (the classifier error rate upper bound) is not examined; also the distinction between isotonic and beta is clear, but differences among isotonic, histogram binning, and Platt on some datasets are within confidence intervals.

The writing contains several typos and minor issues (e.g., 'expeirments', 'tigher', duplicated phrase in Appendix D.2.1), and some results (Theorem 3 applied via hard-label averaging, m large) are stated without quantitative numerical illustration connecting sigma = 1/(2 sqrt(m)) to the bounds.

Impact is confined to the fairly narrow sub-area of Bayes error estimation; the paper does not connect the results to broader questions (e.g., what these estimates mean for multi-class problems, which is deferred to future work).

strengths: The paper is technically careful and clearly written. Theorem 1 provides a genuinely sharper bias analysis of the hard-label-based estimator than Ishida et al. (2023), removing the unnatural dependence on n and revealing an adaptive decay rate that mixes 1/m and 1/√m terms; the computable Corollary 2 (a >200x tighter bound on binarized CIFAR-10) is a practically meaningful improvement.

The extension to corrupted soft labels is a well-motivated new problem setting, and the consistency guarantee via isotonic calibration (Theorem 2) with a weaker 'order-only' assumption is a clean, non-trivial result. The derivation of a high-probability risk bound for binary isotonic regression (Proposition 2) under model misspecification is a useful standalone contribution.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough: synthetic validation of the bias decay rate, multiple real-world datasets (CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H, ChaosNLI), a novel ICLR peer-review dataset, and a principled comparison of calibration algorithms using the FeeBee framework. Code and detailed appendices support reproducibility.
The paper honestly discusses limitations (e.g., the f' >= c assumption of Theorem 3, empirical investigation of order breakage in Appendix D.5).
weaknesses: The contribution is largely incremental over a single prior work (Ishida et al., 2023). The bias analysis in Section 2 follows directly from an existing sharpened Jensen inequality (Gao et al., 2019), and Section 3 is a calibration recipe assembled from classical isotonic regression theory. For a top-tier venue, the conceptual novelty is moderate.

Part of the motivation is weaker than presented: the claim that 'calibration guarantee is not enough' (Example 2) essentially restates the well-known fact that calibration is a weak notion (the paper itself cites this). The example with a constant predictor is trivial and overstates the insight.

The key assumption of Theorem 2/3 — that corrupted soft labels preserve (or approximately preserve, with derivative bounded below) the order of the clean posteriors — is strong and may well fail in the very scenarios motivating the work (LLM annotators, subjective human confidence, CIFAR-10 vs. CIFAR-10H labeling shift). The theory therefore offers limited support for the headline real-world applications.

Theorem 3's bound contains a non-vanishing σ term, so it does not establish consistency for fixed noise; the framing as 'consistent' is somewhat overstated, and the gap between assumption and the empirical regime (Appendix D.2 shows good performance even when the assumption is violated) is left unresolved theoretically.

A methodological concern: the same hard labels y_i are used both to calibrate the soft labels and (through the calibrated labels) in the final estimator, with no discussion of the resulting dependence or overfitting of the calibration step; no split-sample or debiased variant is considered.

Scope is restricted to binary classification, while the most prominent benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10H) are multi-class and require manual binarization; the paper does not explain how the approach would extend to the multi-class setting.

For real-world datasets there is no ground truth for the Bayes error, so the main empirical claims rest on plausibility arguments (estimates near SOTA test error) and FeeBee scores; the CIFAR-10 experiment in particular has essentially no way to distinguish all calibrated methods, all of which produce estimates tightly clustered around the ViT reference.

strengths: The paper makes a clear and well-motivated two-part contribution: (1) a sharper, distribution-adaptive bias bound for the hard-label-based Bayes error estimator (Theorem 1) that removes the unnatural dependence on n and reveals a mixture of 1/m and 1/sqrt(m) decay rates depending on class separation, and (2) a new problem setting — Bayes error estimation from corrupted soft labels — with a provably consistent estimator based on isotonic calibration (Theorems 2 and 3).

The theoretical analysis is technically solid and self-contained. The proof of the isotonic-calibration consistency result develops a new risk bound for binary isotonic regression (Proposition 2), extending sharp oracle inequalities (e.g., Bellec 2018) to Bernoulli noise via a clean generalized localized-width lemma, and the Jensen-gap-based bias analysis is careful. The computable bound (Corollary 2) is a nice practical addition, giving >200x tighter guarantees on binarized CIFAR-10.

The empirical evaluation is thorough and appropriately designed: synthetic experiments with controlled corruption functions validate the theory, real-world datasets (CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H, ChaosNLI, and a new ICLR peer-review dataset) test the method, and the use of the FeeBee framework addresses the key difficulty of comparing estimators when the true Bayes error is unknown.

The paper is honest about limitations (e.g., the failure of beta calibration, violations of the f' >= c assumption in Theorem 3, and order-breakage analysis in Appendix D.5), includes a reproducibility statement with code, and clearly discloses LLM usage.

The instance-free property and the corrupted-soft-label setting are practically relevant, connecting to real issues such as labeling distribution shift (CIFAR-10H), human/LLM annotator subjectivity, and privacy constraints.
weaknesses: The scope is narrow: the paper is restricted to binary classification, and the authors acknowledge that extension to the multi-class case is nontrivial and left to future work. This limits the potential impact on the broader community.

The contribution is primarily incremental over Ishida et al. (2023): the new estimator is a straightforward composition of a classical calibration algorithm (isotonic regression, Zadrozny and Elkan 2002) with the existing plug-in estimator, and the theory leans heavily on existing isotonic regression risk bounds (Zhang 2002; Chatterjee et al. 2015; Bellec 2018; Yang and Barber 2019). The n^{-1/3} rate is the standard minimax rate for isotonic regression, and the constants in the theorems are unspecified.

The key assumptions may be strong in practice: Theorem 2 requires the corruption to be an order-preserving (monotone) function of the clean soft labels, and Theorem 3 additionally requires a bounded derivative. Real corruption processes (human subjectivity, LLM annotation biases, labeling shifts) are not obviously monotone, and while the order-breakage experiments in Appendix D.5 are informative, there is no theory for the violated case.

The practical benefit of the improved bias bound (Section 2) is a refinement rather than a new method; the estimator itself is unchanged, and the consistency improvement for well-separated classes may have limited utility when m (labels per instance) is small.

Some experimental conclusions rest on indirect evidence: for real-world datasets, the 'good' estimates are judged against a classifier's test error or FeeBee scores rather than a known ground truth, so the claim that the calibration-based estimator recovers the true Bayes error is only weakly verified. Additionally, the new ICLR peer-review dataset construction (normalizing reviewer scores to a soft label) is heuristic and its validity as a proxy for the true posterior is not established.
